newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - Sinn Fein eyes British election seats.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Sinn Fein eyes British election seats.

text.p: Sinn Fein, the political arm of IRA guerrillas, is rapping at the door of the British parliament for seats it will never take in a country whose rule over Northern Ireland it does not recognise.

Rooted in revolution, but proclaiming that it espouses peace, Sinn Fein is contesting the British election on May 1 to throw the spotlight on what it says is wide support for its policy to unite the British province with the Irish republic.
Party strategists believe it could capture at least two of the 18 British parliamentary seats at stake in Northern Ireland and present the next British government with a headache.

Current British policy, backed by both the Conservative Party of Prime Minister John Major and his likely successor, opposition Labour Party leader Tony Blair, is to shun contact with Sinn Fein until the IRA ends its 25-year guerrilla war.
The Irish Republican Army has struck in Britain and Northern Ireland several times since abandoning a 17-month truce in February last year, killing two soldiers.

A bomb warning, widely believed to have been from the IRA, caused the postponement of the Grand National, Britain's premier steeplechase horse race, on Saturday, the latest in a series of IRA actions to punctuate the British election campaign.
Sinn Fein says it is committed to talks to end 28 years of strife costing more than 3,200 lives in Northern Ireland, even though it is banned from them until the IRA renews its truce.
"Our position is that we want to see an end to all armed actions," says Martin McGuinness, Sinn Fein's senior strategist who accuses Britain of repressing the region's nationalists.

Political analysts believe the next British prime minister will find it difficult to maintain a contact ban on an elected Sinn Fein legislator, even if he does not claim his seat in the British parliament.
"Even one M.P.(member of parliament) elected, I think will help push the door open," a Sinn Fein insider said.
DISTRUST OF SINN FEIN

Sinn Fein president Gerry Adams won a British parliamentary seat in 1983 but refused to occupy it because it would have entailed allegiance to Britain, whose rule of Northern Ireland he says is an illegal, colonial throwback which must be ended.
Claiming the mantle of radicals of 200 years ago who aimed to unite "Catholic, Protestant and Dissenter" in an Ireland free of British influence, Sinn Fein evokes suspicion in London.

In Dublin, Ireland's government and all its mainstream parties say IRA violence only deepens divisions and delays Irish unity. Northern Ireland's majority Protestants say the republicans are determined to deny them their right to be British citizens.
In 1972 McGuinness and Gerry Adams were flown to London to take part in top-secret, abortive, IRA talks with a British cabinet minister at a house in fashionable Chelsea.
No longer "young turks", they are Sinn Fein's 40-something chief tacticians declaiming against British "intransigence".
They are the public face of a party that has evolved from a "physical force tradition" ingrained in Irish politics.

Adams gave Sinn Fein a major boost winning the West Belfast parliamentary seat in 1983. He held it until 1992 when he was dislodged by the main Catholic Social Democratic and Labour Party. The SDLP has four members of parliament. Sinn Fein has none.
But Sinn Fein has some 50 municipal councillors across Nothern Ireland and elections last year saw its share of the vote rise to 15.5 percent.

"My suspicion is that the SDLP will probably hold very strongly the majority of the nationalist vote but you could see Adams and McGuinness gaining seats," said Richard English, reader in politics at Queen's University in Belfast.
"Sinn Fein might also have a couple of near-misses. They will certainly be a major player after the election."
HISTORICAL BACKGROUND
Sinn Fein was at its peak in 1918 winning a landslide in the last all-Ireland poll for seats in Britain's parliament. The new MPs refused to take seats in London's lower House of Commons.

Sein Fein regarded the victory as a mandate for freedom and formed an underground provisional government while a bitter war with British forces unfolded. A partition settlement won independence for most of the island of Ireland in 1922.

As the fledgling nation spiralled into a cycle of civil war and political splits after partition, other parties emerged. Sinn Fein, clinging to a policy, now abandonded, of boycotting the Dublin parliament, became a political rump.
Sinn Fein existed in the shadows of an IRA that regarded Dublin ministers as traitors and the British as oppressors.

In 1955 Northern Ireland Catholics registered a huge protest against the Protestant-run local administration by casting 150,000 votes for 12 Sinn Fein election candidates, electing two "abstentionists" to parliament.

"You get the feeling that when nationalists want to send a message to Britain they vote for the most extreme party," said Eamon Phoenix, an historian who specialises in Northern Ireland nationalist politics.
The 1981 election to parliament of Bobby Sands, a convicted IRA man, marked the revival of modern Sinn Fein. Sands achieved worldwide fame as leader of a hunger-strike for political prisoner status.
He died on the 66th day of a fast that claimed the lives of nine other prisoners.
